regiones/mesopotamia/resumen.texto: The land between the Tigris and the Euphrates, in present-day Iraq, where the first cities and cuneiform writing emerged. Sumerians, Akkadians, Babylonians and Assyrians left hundreds of thousands of clay tablets that make it possible to study their economy, laws and literature firsthand.

regiones/mesopotamia/eras.11.nombre.texto: Persian, Hellenistic, Parthian and Sasanian rule

regiones/mesopotamia/eras.18.nombre.texto: Republic of Iraq: coups and Baathist rule

regiones/mesopotamia/eras.0.resumen.texto: The first cities (Uruk) appear and, toward the end, cuneiform writing.

regiones/mesopotamia/eras.1.resumen.texto: Final stage of the protohistory of southern Mesopotamia (c. 3100–2900 BC), which follows Uruk and leads into the Early Dynastic period; it brings proto-cuneiform tablets, cylinder seals and polychrome pottery.

regiones/mesopotamia/eras.2.resumen.texto: Rival Sumerian city-states such as Ur, Lagash, Kish and Uruk.

regiones/mesopotamia/eras.3.resumen.texto: Sargon of Akkad unifies Mesopotamia under the first empire of a Semitic language.

regiones/mesopotamia/eras.4.resumen.texto: After the fall of the Akkadian Empire, kings of Gutian origin (from the Zagros mountains) ruled part of Mesopotamia until Utu-hengal of Uruk and Ur-Nammu of Ur displaced them, around 2112 BC. How long their rule lasted and how far it extended is debated (from a few years to a century), and they left almost no inscriptions.

regiones/mesopotamia/eras.5.resumen.texto: A Sumerian revival with a well-documented bureaucratic state.

regiones/mesopotamia/eras.6.resumen.texto: Babylonian hegemony under Hammurabi and his law code.

regiones/mesopotamia/eras.7.resumen.texto: A dynasty of uncertain origin (perhaps from the Zagros) ruled Babylon from shortly after 1595 BC (middle chronology; 1531 in the short chronology) until 1155 BC, the longest of its history. It preserved Babylonian traditions, while Mitanni and then Assyria rose to the north.

regiones/mesopotamia/eras.8.resumen.texto: After the fall of the Kassites to Elam (1155 BC), Babylon was ruled by the Second Dynasty of Isin (with Nebuchadnezzar I) and other short-lived dynasties, while Arameans and Chaldeans settled in. Assyria, a power from around 1365 BC, retreated until its neo-Assyrian revival in 911.

regiones/mesopotamia/eras.9.resumen.texto: Assyria dominates the Near East from Nineveh, Nimrud and Dur-Sharrukin.

regiones/mesopotamia/eras.10.resumen.texto: Nebuchadnezzar II rebuilds Babylon; the empire falls to Cyrus.

regiones/mesopotamia/eras.11.resumen.texto: Mesopotamia passes from empire to empire until the Arab conquest in 637.

regiones/mesopotamia/eras.12.resumen.texto: Arab armies take Sasanian Iraq (Qadisiyya around 636, Ctesiphon in 637). Kufa and Basra, founded as garrison camps, become centers of the caliphate, with Damascus as the Umayyad capital from 661.

regiones/mesopotamia/eras.13.resumen.texto: The Abbasids govern from Baghdad, founded in 762, the caliphate at its cultural peak. From the 10th century real power passes to the Buyids and then to the Seljuks, until the Mongol sack of 1258.

regiones/mesopotamia/eras.14.resumen.texto: After the Mongol capture of Baghdad (1258), the country passes through the Ilkhanate, the Jalayirids, Tamerlane’s invasion (1401), the Turkmen confederations Kara Koyunlu and Ak Koyunlu, and from 1508 the Safavids.

regiones/mesopotamia/eras.15.resumen.texto: Suleiman the Magnificent takes Baghdad in 1534. The Ottomans rule it until 1917, with a Safavid interlude (1623–1638), and divide the country into provinces (Baghdad, Basra, Mosul).

regiones/mesopotamia/eras.16.resumen.texto: Great Britain takes Baghdad in 1917. The San Remo conference assigns it the mandate over Iraq (1920), and the revolt of that year breaks out against it. The British install Faisal I as king (1921), and the mandate is put into effect through the Anglo-Iraqi treaty of 1922, until formal independence in 1932.

regiones/mesopotamia/eras.17.resumen.texto: Iraq achieves formal independence in 1932 as a Hashemite monarchy, under strong British influence, until the 1958 coup.

regiones/mesopotamia/eras.18.resumen.texto: A succession of coups leads to the Baathist regime (from 1968) and the dictatorship of Saddam Hussein (1979–2003), with the wars against Iran (1980–1988) and the Gulf War (1990–1991).

regiones/mesopotamia/eras.19.resumen.texto: The US-led invasion overthrows the regime in 2003 and opens a period of occupation, insurgency, sectarian war and the fight against the Islamic State.

regiones/mesopotamia/religiones.3.nota.texto: Shiites are the majority in present-day Iraq (estimates put them at around 60%). There is no recent religious census, and the north is mostly Sunni and Kurdish.

regiones/mesopotamia/culturas.3.nota.texto: With a significant Kurdish minority in the north.

regiones/mesopotamia/culturas.4.nota.texto: Kurds are a significant minority in the north of the country, with an autonomous region; there is no recent census giving figures.

regiones/mesopotamia/idiomas.3.nota.texto: Kurdish is an official language in the autonomous Kurdistan Region.

regiones/mesopotamia/idiomas.4.nota.texto: Official language in the autonomous Kurdistan Region; spoken in the north.

regiones/levante/resumen.texto: The eastern strip of the Mediterranean, between Anatolia and Egypt: today Syria, Lebanon, Israel, Palestine and Jordan. It was a corridor between the great empires and the cradle of alphabets, of Judaism, of Christianity and of trading cities such as Byblos and Tyre.

regiones/levante/eras.0.resumen.texto: City-states such as Byblos, Ugarit and Hazor, under Egyptian and Mesopotamian influence.

regiones/levante/eras.1.resumen.texto: Israel, Judah, the Aramean kingdoms and the Phoenician cities emerge.

regiones/levante/eras.2.resumen.texto: Babylonian exile and return under the Achaemenid Empire.

regiones/levante/eras.3.resumen.texto: After Alexander, the Levant is contested between the Ptolemies and the Seleucids.

regiones/levante/eras.4.resumen.texto: Rome annexes the region; Christianity spreads from Judea.

regiones/levante/eras.5.resumen.texto: Arab conquest of Syria and Palestine; Damascus is the Umayyad capital.

regiones/levante/eras.6.resumen.texto: Crusaders and Muslims fight over Jerusalem and the coast.

regiones/levante/eras.7.resumen.texto: The Mamluks of Cairo, masters of the Syrian interior from 1260 (Ayn Jalut), take Acre in 1291 and govern the whole Levant until the Ottoman conquest of 1516. They resist the Mongols, and suffer the Black Death and Tamerlane’s sack of Damascus (1400–1401).

regiones/levante/eras.8.resumen.texto: Syria, Lebanon and Palestine are part of the Ottoman Empire until the First World War.

regiones/levante/eras.9.resumen.texto: After the Allied military occupation (1918–1920) and the fall of the short-lived Arab Kingdom of Syria (1920), France receives the mandates for Syria and Lebanon, and Great Britain those for Palestine and Transjordan. The Palestine mandate incorporates the Balfour Declaration (1917), which supported a “national home for the Jewish people.” It was followed by Jewish immigration, the Arab revolt of 1936–1939 and the UN partition plan (1947). Lebanon became independent in 1943, Syria and Transjordan in 1946, and the Palestine mandate ended in 1948.

regiones/levante/eras.10.resumen.texto: Syria, Lebanon and Jordan are already independent (1943–1946). In 1948 Israel is proclaimed; the 1948 war (the War of Independence for Israelis, the Nakba for Palestinians) leaves more than 700,000 Palestinian refugees. Wars follow in 1967 (with Israel’s occupation of the West Bank, Gaza and the Golan, as the UN calls it) and in 1973, the Lebanese civil war (1975–1990), the Syrian civil war from 2011, which toppled Assad in 2024, and the Gaza war since Hamas’s attack of October 2023.

regiones/levante/demografia.0.nota.texto: Sum of Israel, Palestine, Lebanon, Syria and Jordan, that is, of the four regions of the Levant.

regiones/levante/religiones.3.nombre.texto: Pagan religions of the Greco-Roman Levant

regiones/levante/religiones.4.nombre.texto: Judaism (after the destruction of the Temple)

regiones/levante/religiones.1.nota.texto: From the Iron Age, with the Yahwism of Israel and Judah alongside the Canaanite cults. How many people practiced it exclusively, and when monotheism became established, are debated.

regiones/levante/religiones.3.nota.texto: Local Syrian and Phoenician cults (Baal, Atargatis, Jupiter Heliopolitanus) blended with Greco-Roman ones. There are no censuses, and the usual estimate in historiography is that they were the majority.

regiones/levante/religiones.4.nota.texto: After 70 and the defeat of Bar Kokhba (135), the Jewish population shifted to Galilee, where the Mishnah (c. 200) and then the Jerusalem Talmud were compiled. In Judea, Jews were expelled from Jerusalem (Aelia Capitolina).

regiones/levante/religiones.5.nota.texto: Communities in Jerusalem, Antioch and along the coast; Christianity became the majority only after Constantine.

regiones/levante/religiones.7.nota.texto: This holds for the Levant as a whole: in Israel Judaism predominates, and in Lebanon and Syria there are significant Christian, Shiite, Alawite and Druze communities.

regiones/levante/religiones.8.nota.texto: It is the religion of most of Israel’s population; across the Levant as a whole it weighs less than Islam.

regiones/levante/culturas.0.nombre.texto: Canaanite and other Semitic Bronze Age cultures

regiones/levante/culturas.0.nota.texto: The Canaanite city-states (Byblos, Ugarit, Hazor) and Ebla; Israelite culture appears only in the Iron Age.

regiones/levante/culturas.4.nota.texto: It predominates in Israel; across the Levant as a whole it weighs less than Arab culture.

regiones/levante/idiomas.0.nombre.texto: Barely documented Semitic languages (Eblaite at Ebla, c. 2500–2250 BC)

regiones/levante/idiomas.1.nombre.texto: Amorite and Old Canaanite (personal names, Proto-Sinaitic, Amarna glosses); Akkadian as written language

regiones/levante/idiomas.2.nombre.texto: Canaanite languages (Hebrew, Phoenician, Moabite) and Aramaic

regiones/levante/idiomas.3.nombre.texto: Aramaic (with Greek as the language of administration)

regiones/levante/idiomas.0.nota.texto: There is almost no writing in the region before Ebla; Eblaite is an East Semitic language, distinct from Canaanite.

regiones/levante/idiomas.1.nota.texto: Almost everything is known from personal names, glosses in letters written in Akkadian (Amarna) and the Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions; the spoken languages are poorly documented.

regiones/levante/idiomas.4.nota.texto: In Israel the majority language is Hebrew.

regiones/levante/idiomas.5.nota.texto: It is the majority language in Israel; across the Levant as a whole it weighs less than Arabic.

regiones/anatolia/resumen.texto: The peninsula of Asia Minor, a bridge between Europe and Asia: present-day Asian Turkey. It was home to the Hittite Empire, Troy, Lydia, the Greek cities of Ionia and, later, Byzantium and the Ottoman Empire.

regiones/anatolia/eras.0.nombre.texto: Assyrian colonies and Anatolian kingdoms before the Hittite Empire

regiones/anatolia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Assyrian merchants maintain trading colonies (karum), such as the one at Kanesh, until around 1700 BC, while local kingdoms such as Kussara and Neša fight one another; from them emerges the Old Hittite Kingdom around 1650.

regiones/anatolia/eras.1.resumen.texto: From Hattusa, the Hittites compete with Egypt and Assyria for control of the Near East.

regiones/anatolia/eras.2.resumen.texto: After the collapse of the Bronze Age, Phrygia (Midas) and Lydia (Croesus) emerge.

regiones/anatolia/eras.3.resumen.texto: Cyrus conquers Lydia, and the Greek cities of the coast become satrapies.

regiones/anatolia/eras.4.resumen.texto: Alexander conquers it; then the Seleucids, Pergamon and other kingdoms rule.

regiones/anatolia/eras.5.resumen.texto: Rome creates the province of Asia; Christianity spreads through Paul, and the Council of Nicaea is held.

regiones/anatolia/eras.6.resumen.texto: The Battle of Manzikert opens Anatolia to the Turks.

regiones/anatolia/eras.7.resumen.texto: The Ottomans control Anatolia and conquer Constantinople in 1453.

regiones/anatolia/eras.8.resumen.texto: Atatürk founds the republic with its capital in Ankara. Turkey in the 21st century, with the process of accession to the European Union since 2005 and AKP governments since 2002.

regiones/anatolia/demografia.0.nota.texto: All of Turkey, with Eastern Thrace and historical Western Armenia.

regiones/anatolia/religiones.0.nota.texto: The Kültepe texts are mainly commercial and name few gods; the religion of the period is known mainly from later Hittite texts.

regiones/anatolia/religiones.4.nota.texto: From Paul's missions. Around 112, Pliny the Younger wrote from Bithynia that Christianity had spread through cities, villages and countryside, and that the temples were almost abandoned (Letters X.96).

regiones/anatolia/religiones.5.nota.texto: In Phrygia there are 3rd-century epitaphs that declare the faith of the deceased, those of “Christians for Christians” (Gibson, 1978), and Eusebius (Ecclesiastical History VIII.11) recounts that during Diocletian's persecution an entire Phrygian city, whose inhabitants were Christians, was burned.

regiones/anatolia/religiones.6.nota.texto: From 325 Christianity is counted as the majority (see its note). Traditional cults continued until the laws of Theodosius that banned sacrifices and closed the temples (391-392).

regiones/anatolia/religiones.7.nota.texto: There are no figures for believers: the shift to a majority in 325, the year of the Council of Nicaea, is a conventional cut-off. Asia Minor was among the most Christianized regions of the Empire, and Stark's model (The Rise of Christianity, 1996) gives 10% Christians for the whole Empire around 300 and more than half by 350. From that year polytheism is counted as significant, so that there are not two majority religions at once.

regiones/anatolia/religiones.8.nota.texto: John of Ephesus recounts that in 542, sent by Justinian, he baptized seventy thousand pagans in Asia Minor.

regiones/anatolia/religiones.9.nota.texto: With a significant Alevi minority; there is no religious census.

regiones/anatolia/culturas.0.nombre.texto: Hattic, Hittite and Luwian (with Assyrian trading colonies)

regiones/anatolia/culturas.4.nota.texto: Three Celtic peoples settled on the central plateau from around 275 BC.

regiones/anatolia/culturas.5.nota.texto: With a significant Kurdish minority in the east.

regiones/anatolia/culturas.6.nota.texto: Significant minority in the east and southeast; the figures are estimates.

regiones/anatolia/idiomas.3.nombre.texto: Phrygian, Lydian, Luwian and Ionian Greek

regiones/anatolia/idiomas.0.nota.texto: Hattic is not Indo-European and dies out early; Hittite, Luwian and Palaic are Anatolian.

regiones/anatolia/idiomas.1.nota.texto: Language of the some 23,000 commercial tablets from Kültepe, written by Assyrian merchants. After the colonies, Akkadian returns to the region as the written language of the Hittite chancery (bilingual annals and testament of Hattusili I, around 1650-1620 BC, and later diplomatic correspondence).

regiones/anatolia/idiomas.3.nota.texto: Lydian and Luwian are Anatolian languages; Phrygian and Greek are other Indo-European branches. They are grouped in the Anatolian family because that is the family that predominates in the region.

regiones/anatolia/idiomas.6.nota.texto: Kurdish is spoken in the east.

regiones/anatolia/idiomas.7.nota.texto: It is spoken in the east and southeast.

regiones/grecia/resumen.texto: The Aegean world: mainland Greece, the Aegean islands and Crete. The city-states gave rise to democracy, philosophy, theater and historiography, and Greek culture later spread throughout the eastern Mediterranean.

regiones/grecia/eras.7.nombre.texto: Ottoman conquest (Morea and Athens, as tributaries)

regiones/grecia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Walled villages, Minyan pottery and cist graves on mainland Greece (around 2000-1600 BC), while in Crete the Minoan civilization of palaces flourishes, with Linear A script (1800-1450 BC); the shaft graves of Mycenae mark the transition to the Mycenaean civilization.

regiones/grecia/eras.1.resumen.texto: Fortified palaces such as Mycenae and Pylos; Linear B script, the oldest known form of Greek.

regiones/grecia/eras.2.resumen.texto: The polis, the alphabet, the Homeric poems and colonies emerge.

regiones/grecia/eras.3.resumen.texto: Athens and Sparta; the Persian and Peloponnesian Wars; Plato and Aristotle.

regiones/grecia/eras.4.resumen.texto: The successor kingdoms of Alexander; mainland Greece falls under Macedon.

regiones/grecia/eras.5.resumen.texto: Rome conquers Greece but adopts its culture.

regiones/grecia/eras.6.resumen.texto: Greek continuity under the Orthodox Christian Byzantine Empire.

regiones/grecia/eras.7.resumen.texto: After the fall of Constantinople (1453), the Despotate of Morea and the Duchy of Athens survive by paying tribute to Mehmed II; the Ottomans take Athens in 1456 and its Acropolis in 1458, and conquer the Morea in 1460.

regiones/grecia/eras.8.resumen.texto: Athens falls in 1458; Greece is an Ottoman province.

regiones/grecia/eras.9.resumen.texto: War of independence (1821) and creation of the Greek state in 1832.

regiones/grecia/religiones.0.nombre.texto: Minoan religion (peak and cave sanctuaries; no legible texts)

regiones/grecia/religiones.0.nota.texto: Applies only to Crete: it is reconstructed from archaeology (palaces, peak sanctuaries, sacred caves, seals and paintings), and the names of its gods are not known. No record survives of the religion of mainland Middle Helladic Greece.

regiones/grecia/culturas.0.nota.texto: Middle Helladic culture on the mainland and Minoan culture on Crete, grouped in the European Bronze Age family rather than the Greek one, because the language of the Minoans (Linear A) is undeciphered and when Greek reached the peninsula is debated (from around 2200 BC to shortly before 1600, depending on the authors).

regiones/grecia/idiomas.0.nombre.texto: Proto-Greek and languages of the pre-Hellenic substratum

regiones/grecia/idiomas.1.nombre.texto: Minoan (Linear A and Cretan hieroglyphs, undeciphered)

regiones/grecia/idiomas.0.nota.texto: Greek is attested from the Linear B texts (around 1450 BC); before that there is no writing on the mainland, and the pre-Hellenic substratum (place names ending in -nthos or -ssos) indicates that other languages were spoken, whose nature is debated.

regiones/grecia/idiomas.1.nota.texto: Language of Minoan Crete; Linear A was used from 1800 to 1450 BC and is undeciphered, so it is not known what family it belonged to.

regiones/italia/resumen.texto: The Italian peninsula (without the islands), where Rome was born and went on to unify the Mediterranean under its rule. From antiquity to the present it has been a crossroads of Etruscans, Greeks, Romans, the Catholic Church and the cities of the Renaissance.

regiones/italia/eras.3.nombre.texto: Pre-Roman Italy and the Roman monarchy

regiones/italia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Farmers with impressed pottery in the south from around 6000 BC and in the north from around 5500 BC.

regiones/italia/eras.1.resumen.texto: First copper objects; Ötzi, the Iceman, died in the Alps of South Tyrol around 3300 BC.

regiones/italia/eras.2.resumen.texto: Pile dwellings and terramare in the north, Apennine culture in the center and south, and contacts with the Mycenaeans.

regiones/italia/eras.3.resumen.texto: Etruscans, Latins and Greeks of Magna Graecia; according to tradition, Rome is founded in 753 BC.

regiones/italia/eras.4.resumen.texto: Rome dominates Italy and then the Mediterranean, and collapses into civil wars.

regiones/italia/eras.5.resumen.texto: From Augustus to the deposition of Romulus Augustulus in 476.

regiones/italia/eras.6.resumen.texto: Italy is divided between Germanic peoples and the Byzantine Empire.

regiones/italia/eras.7.resumen.texto: Frankish rule, the Papal States and the rise of independent communes.

regiones/italia/eras.8.resumen.texto: Florence, Venice and Milan; flourishing of art and letters, and the Italian Wars.

regiones/italia/eras.9.resumen.texto: Spanish, Austrians and French control much of the peninsula.

regiones/italia/eras.10.resumen.texto: Kingdom of Italy from 1861 and Republic from 1946. The Italian Republic in the 21st century, within the European Union and the eurozone.

regiones/italia/demografia.0.nota.texto: All of Italy (with Sicily and Sardinia), San Marino, Vatican City and Malta.

regiones/italia/demografia.10.nota.texto: It is not the population: it is the list of men fit for arms in Rome and its allies at the Gallic invasion of 225 BC, more than 700,000 infantry and 70,000 cavalry. Unlike rhetorical figures, it is usually thought to come from Roman records, perhaps through Fabius Pictor, who fought in that war and, according to Orosius (IV.13.6), gave 800,000 men under arms. Brunt (Italian Manpower, 1971) uses it as a basis for calculating Italy's free population, but how to read its entries and how many people it implies in total is disputed.

regiones/italia/demografia.12.nota.texto: With Sicily and Sardinia, which this region does not have. Mid-2nd century.

regiones/italia/demografia.14.nota.texto: With Sicily and Sardinia, which this region does not have. Traditional reading of Augustus's censuses (“low count”).

regiones/italia/demografia.15.nota.texto: With Sicily and Sardinia, which this region does not have. Revised reading of Augustus's censuses (“high count”, by Lo Cascio).

regiones/italia/demografia.16.nota.texto: All of Italy, with Sicily and Sardinia.

regiones/italia/demografia.18.nota.texto: All of Italy. Urlanis (1941) gives 7 million.

regiones/italia/demografia.19.nota.texto: All of Italy. Urlanis (1941) gives 10 million in 1300 and 8 million in 1350.

regiones/italia/demografia.20.nota.texto: All of Italy. Urlanis (1941) gives 10.5 million.

regiones/italia/religiones.3.nota.texto: Nominal majority; regular practice and the Orthodox, Protestant, Muslim and non-believing minorities have grown.

regiones/italia/culturas.3.nombre.texto: Latin and Italic (Latins, Sabines, Umbrians, Oscans, Samnites)

regiones/italia/culturas.0.nota.texto: Farmers who descended mostly from those of Anatolia, mixed with local hunter-gatherers (Haak et al. 2015).

regiones/italia/culturas.3.nota.texto: The largest by extent: the Italic-speaking peoples occupied most of the peninsula.

regiones/italia/culturas.4.nota.texto: From the Villanova culture (9th century BC); the Etruscans dominate Etruria, part of the Po plain and Campania, and Rome absorbs them between the 4th and 1st centuries BC.

regiones/italia/idiomas.4.nombre.texto: Oscan, Umbrian and other Italic languages

regiones/italia/idiomas.0.nota.texto: Nobody knows what languages the Neolithic farmers spoke: they left no texts. They are assumed to predate the Indo-European ones because genetics shows that these arrived later, with people of Steppe ancestry; their traces are sought in place names and loanwords, with much-disputed theories.

regiones/italia/idiomas.1.nota.texto: No texts. That they were Indo-European is inferred from the arrival of people of Steppe ancestry (Haak et al. 2015; Olalde et al. 2018) and from the fact that the first documented languages of the area are Indo-European; when and where Proto-Celtic arose is debated (Koch and Cunliffe: the Atlantic in the Bronze Age; Sims-Williams 2020: Bronze Age Gaul, between the centre and the west of Europe).

regiones/italia/idiomas.3.nota.texto: Until the 4th century BC it was spoken only in Latium.

regiones/italia/idiomas.4.nota.texto: Predominant by extent in the center and south of the Apennines; Latin, also Italic, is treated separately. Oscan was written until the 1st century.

regiones/italia/idiomas.5.nota.texto: About thirteen thousand inscriptions, from around 700 BC to the 1st century; they can be read, but are understood only in part. Emperor Claudius wrote a history of the Etruscans that has been lost.

regiones/italia/idiomas.13.nota.texto: Whether today's Griko comes from Magna Graecia (Rohlfs) or from the Byzantine period (Battisti) is debated.

regiones/persia/resumen.texto: The Iranian Plateau, center of the Persian empires: Achaemenid, Parthian and Sasanian. It gave rise to the first empire that united Egypt, Mesopotamia and Central Asia, and to Zoroastrianism, which influenced later religions.

regiones/persia/eras.2.nombre.texto: Alexander's conquest and the wars of the Diadochi

regiones/persia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Elam in the southwest; Medes and Persians appear in Assyrian sources from the 9th century BC.

regiones/persia/eras.1.resumen.texto: Cyrus, Darius and Xerxes rule from Persepolis and Susa until Alexander's conquest.

regiones/persia/eras.2.resumen.texto: Alexander the Great takes Persepolis and Ecbatana (330 BC) and dies in 323; his generals fight over Iran until Seleucus establishes himself in Babylon (312 BC) and founds the Seleucid Empire.

regiones/persia/eras.3.resumen.texto: Hellenistic rule, then the Parthian Empire of the Arsacids.

regiones/persia/eras.4.resumen.texto: Persia is officially Zoroastrian and a rival of Rome and Byzantium, until the Arab conquest.

regiones/persia/eras.5.resumen.texto: Persia becomes Islamic; Persian is revived in the poetry of Ferdowsi.

regiones/persia/eras.6.resumen.texto: Turkish and Mongol rule, with great Persian literature.

regiones/persia/eras.7.resumen.texto: The Safavids convert Iran to Twelver Shiism.

regiones/persia/eras.8.resumen.texto: Pahlavi dynasty and, from 1979, the Islamic Republic.

regiones/persia/idiomas.2.nombre.texto: Persian in transition from Old to Middle

regiones/persia/idiomas.5.nombre.texto: Middle Persian (Pahlavi) and early forms of New Persian

regiones/persia/idiomas.2.nota.texto: Old Persian cuneiform disappears with the Achaemenids, and there are almost no Iranian texts until Middle Persian; the transition between the two stages is poorly documented.

regiones/persia/idiomas.3.nota.texto: Language of the conquerors and the new administration; Imperial Aramaic remained the language of the chancery.

regiones/persia/idiomas.5.nota.texto: Pahlavi remained in use (Zoroastrian literature was largely fixed in the 9th and 10th centuries). The first New Persian texts are Judeo-Persian from the 8th century (a letter from Dandan Oilik, dated 718, and the inscription of Tang-e Azao, 752-753); what begins in the 9th century is literature in the Arabic script. In between there are few texts.

regiones/persia/idiomas.6.nota.texto: According to the historiographical tradition, al-Hajjaj moved the chancery of Iraq from Persian to Arabic in 697, and that of Khurasan moved to Arabic around 742; in the countryside Iranian continued to be spoken.

regiones/china/resumen.texto: The historical core of China, in the basins of the Yellow River and the Yangtze. One of the oldest civilizations developed there, with continuous writing since the Shang oracle bones, a bureaucratic state since the Qin and Han, and a very rich historical and philosophical tradition.

regiones/china/eras.3.nombre.texto: Spring and Autumn and Warring States

regiones/china/eras.5.nombre.texto: Three Kingdoms and Northern and Southern dynasties

regiones/china/eras.0.resumen.texto: Erlitou culture, in the Yellow River valley, with palaces and ritual bronzes; Chinese archaeology identifies it with the Xia of tradition, something several Western authors consider premature because there are no contemporary writings.

regiones/china/eras.1.resumen.texto: First dynasty with documented writing: inscriptions on oracle bones from Anyang.

regiones/china/eras.2.resumen.texto: The Zhou defeat the Shang and develop the “Mandate of Heaven.”

regiones/china/eras.3.resumen.texto: Political fragmentation and the flourishing of Confucius, Laozi and the “hundred schools.”

regiones/china/eras.4.resumen.texto: Imperial unification by Qin Shi Huang and consolidation of the Confucian state under the Han.

regiones/china/eras.6.resumen.texto: Reunification, openness to the outside world and the golden age of poetry.

regiones/china/eras.7.resumen.texto: After the fall of the Tang (907), five short-lived dynasties follow one another on the central plain, and a dozen kingdoms divide the south, until the Song gradually reunify the country from 960.

regiones/china/eras.8.resumen.texto: Economic and technological development, followed by the Mongol conquest.

regiones/china/eras.9.resumen.texto: The last empires, up to the revolution of 1911-1912.

regiones/china/eras.10.resumen.texto: Follows the Qing in 1912; come the era of the warlords, the nominal unification under the Kuomintang (1928), the Japanese invasion (1937-1945) and the civil war between the Kuomintang and the Communist Party. In 1949 the Communist Party proclaims the People's Republic, and the government of the Republic of China retreats to Taiwan, where it remains to this day.

regiones/china/eras.11.resumen.texto: Founded by the Communist Party in 1949; marked by the Great Leap Forward and the famine of 1959-1961 (15 to 46 million deaths, according to estimates), the Cultural Revolution (1966-1976), Deng Xiaoping's reforms from 1978, the Tiananmen protests of 1989, which the army dissolved, and the economic growth that followed.

regiones/china/demografia.0.nota.texto: All of China (with Tibet, Xinjiang, Manchuria, Inner Mongolia and the south), Hong Kong and Macau.

regiones/china/demografia.10.nota.texto: Census of AD 2 across the entire Han empire, including areas outside this region. 59,594,978 is the total given by the Hanshu; adding up its commanderies yields 57,671,400 people in 12,366,470 households, the figure used by Bielenstein and Nishijima. This is registered population: Ge Jianxiong estimates that the real figure exceeded 65 million.

regiones/china/demografia.11.nota.texto: Census of AD 140 across the entire empire: 9,698,630 households and 49,150,220 people, according to the text of the “Junguo zhi”. Nishijima (1986) rounds it to about 48 million and notes that the drop from AD 2 mainly reflects unregistered people, not a real decline.

regiones/china/religiones.0.nombre.texto: Erlitou rites (divination with bones, ritual bronze vessels)

regiones/china/religiones.2.nombre.texto: Shang religion: ancestors, Di and nature spirits

regiones/china/religiones.0.nota.texto: No texts from the period survive: the ritual bronzes and the palaces of Erlitou suggest an organized cult; what is known about the ancestors and Di comes from Shang oracle bones (around 1250 BC), and Heaven (Tian) is a Zhou concept.

regiones/china/religiones.2.nota.texto: Known from the oracle bones of Anyang, from the reign of Wu Ding onward.

regiones/china/religiones.5.nota.texto: It is practiced in temples of the Han and Tibetan traditions; figures for adherents are disputed because of the difficulty of measuring religion in China.

regiones/china/religiones.6.nota.texto: In surveys few people declare themselves Taoist, because for many Chinese the term designates ordained priests; its rites are also practiced within popular religion.

regiones/china/religiones.7.nota.texto: According to the Pew Research Center (“Measuring Religion in China,” 2023), a minority declares itself religious, although many practice traditional rites; what counts as religion is disputed.

regiones/china/culturas.0.nombre.texto: Erlitou and early Bronze Age cultures

regiones/china/culturas.0.nota.texto: The identification with the Xia is disputed; the cultural continuity with the Shang is what allows it to be placed in this family.

regiones/china/idiomas.3.nombre.texto: Chinese (with Mandarin as the common language)

regiones/china/idiomas.0.nota.texto: The people of Erlitou and the early Shang are presumed to have spoken an ancestor of Old Chinese, but there are no texts: the first writing is that of the oracle bones of Wu Ding (around 1250 BC).

regiones/india/resumen.texto: The north of the Indian subcontinent, between the Indus and the Ganges: cradle of the Indus civilization, the Vedic texts, Buddhism and Jainism, and of empires such as the Maurya and the Gupta. It is one of the regions with the greatest cultural continuity in the world.

regiones/india/eras.2.nombre.texto: Mahajanapadas and the rise of Buddhism

regiones/india/eras.0.resumen.texto: Planned cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa; a script still undeciphered.

regiones/india/eras.1.resumen.texto: Composition of the Vedas and expansion of Indo-Aryan peoples toward the Ganges.

regiones/india/eras.2.resumen.texto: Sixteen kingdoms; the Buddha and Mahavira preach.

regiones/india/eras.3.resumen.texto: Chandragupta and Ashoka unify almost the entire subcontinent.

regiones/india/eras.4.resumen.texto: Indo-Greeks, Scythians and Kushans; growth of Silk Road trade.

regiones/india/eras.5.resumen.texto: Classical age of science and art, followed by regional kingdoms.

regiones/india/eras.8.resumen.texto: The partition of 1947 creates India and Pakistan with mass violence: some 14.5 million people cross the new borders, and estimates of deaths range from 200,000 to 2 million (most specialists accept around one million). India has been a republic since 1950, with the Emergency of 1975-1977 and economic reforms from 1991; Pakistan goes through several military governments; both countries fight over Kashmir (1947-1948, 1965, 1999), and Bangladesh becomes independent from Pakistan after the war of 1971.

regiones/india/demografia.0.nota.texto: All of India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan, including southern India, which has its own region without a series.

regiones/india/religiones.2.nota.texto: In the Pakistani and Bangladeshi parts of the river basins the majority is Muslim.

regiones/india/religiones.4.nota.texto: Pakistan, Bangladesh and the Muslims of northern India make up more than a third of the population of the area; in Pakistan and Bangladesh it is the religion of the great majority.

regiones/india/idiomas.0.nombre.texto: Unknown languages of the late Indus phase (and perhaps the first Indo-Aryan ones)

regiones/india/idiomas.0.nota.texto: The Indus script is undeciphered and it is not known what language its people spoke (proto-Dravidian, Munda and a lost language have been proposed); the Indo-Aryan reading, defended by S. R. Rao, is marginal. Vedic Sanskrit is attested only through the oral tradition of the Rigveda, fixed in writing much later and of disputed dating (from around 1500 BC onward).

regiones/india/idiomas.3.nota.texto: With important Dravidian languages in the south, outside the river basin area.

regiones/mesoamerica/resumen.texto: The cultural area of central and southern Mexico and part of Central America, where the Olmecs, Zapotecs, Maya, Teotihuacanos and Mexica developed. They shared maize cultivation, a 260-day ritual calendar, glyphic writing and the ballgame. Its study combines archaeology, codices and colonial chronicles.

regiones/mesoamerica/eras.0.nombre.texto: Late Archaic and first Formative villages

regiones/mesoamerica/eras.0.resumen.texto: Maize farmers settle in villages with pottery (such as those of Soconusco), before the Olmec civilization of San Lorenzo takes off around 1400-1200 BC.

regiones/mesoamerica/eras.1.resumen.texto: Appearance of the first villages and centers such as San Lorenzo and La Venta (Olmec), and of writing and the calendar.

regiones/mesoamerica/eras.2.resumen.texto: Rise of Teotihuacan, Monte Albán and the Maya cities of the lowlands.

regiones/mesoamerica/eras.3.resumen.texto: Collapse of the classic Maya cities; Tula and Chichén Itzá.

regiones/mesoamerica/eras.4.resumen.texto: The Mexica found Tenochtitlan (1325) and form the Triple Alliance, until the arrival of Cortés.

regiones/mesoamerica/eras.5.resumen.texto: Spanish conquest and colonial society with evangelization.

regiones/mesoamerica/eras.6.resumen.texto: Independence of Mexico and of the Central American republics. The countries of the region in the 21st century, with democratic alternation in Mexico since 2000, migration northward, and the violence of drug trafficking and gangs.

regiones/mesoamerica/demografia.0.nota.texto: All of Mexico (including Aridoamerica), Guatemala, Belize and El Salvador.

regiones/mesoamerica/religiones.0.nota.texto: El Manatí (Veracruz) is a swamp of offerings used since around 1600 BC, with rubber balls, axes and wooden sculptures, and Paso de la Amada has the oldest known ballcourt, around 1650 BC. There are no texts: the meaning of these rites is inferred from the finds.

regiones/mesoamerica/religiones.2.nota.texto: A declared majority, which declines with the growth of Protestantism and of those who declare no religion.

regiones/mesoamerica/culturas.0.nombre.texto: Late Archaic and early Formative agricultural villages

regiones/mesoamerica/culturas.1.nombre.texto: Olmec, Maya, Zapotec, Teotihuacan, Mexica and others

regiones/mesoamerica/culturas.0.nota.texto: There is no writing: what is known comes from archaeology (pottery of Barra and Locona, houses and burials of Paso de la Amada).

regiones/mesoamerica/culturas.2.nota.texto: With a large Indigenous population (about 20% of Mexicans identify as Indigenous, and more in Guatemala) and an Afro-descendant population.

regiones/mesoamerica/idiomas.4.nombre.texto: Current Indigenous languages (Nahuatl, Maya, Zapotec, Mixtec…)

regiones/mesoamerica/idiomas.0.nota.texto: Mesoamerican writing appears in the first millennium BC; historical linguistics reconstructs proto-languages (Proto-Mixe-Zoque, Proto-Otomanguean and others) without being able to pin down where each one was spoken at this time.

regiones/mesoamerica/idiomas.3.nota.texto: With some 60 living Indigenous languages, mainly in Mexico and Guatemala.

regiones/mesoamerica/idiomas.4.nota.texto: They are a minority in the region as a whole, larger in Guatemala and southern Mexico.

regiones/andes/resumen.texto: The coast, highlands and altiplano of present-day Peru and western Bolivia: one of the independent cradles of civilization, with Caral, Chavín, Nazca, Moche, Wari, Tiwanaku and the Inca Empire (Tawantinsuyu). The Incas did not use alphabetic writing but quipus; for this reason, colonial chronicles are the main written source.

regiones/andes/eras.0.resumen.texto: Monumental cities of the north-central coast and the first temples.

regiones/andes/eras.1.resumen.texto: Ceremonial center of Chavín de Huántar, with influence throughout the Andes.

regiones/andes/eras.2.resumen.texto: Regional cultures with great artistic and irrigation works.

regiones/andes/eras.3.resumen.texto: First expansionist states of the southern highlands and the altiplano.

regiones/andes/eras.4.resumen.texto: Chimú kingdom on the north coast; the state of Cusco grows in the highlands.

regiones/andes/eras.5.resumen.texto: Pachacuti begins the expansion; Tawantinsuyu becomes the largest empire in the Americas.

regiones/andes/eras.6.resumen.texto: Spanish conquest; Lima, founded in 1535, is the capital of the viceroyalty, created in 1542. In 1776 Upper Peru passed to the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata.

regiones/andes/demografia.0.nota.texto: All of Peru and Bolivia, including their Amazonian east (which has its own region without a series).

regiones/andes/religiones.0.nombre.texto: Andean religion (worship of the sun, huacas and ancestors)

regiones/andes/idiomas.0.nota.texto: Unwritten: nobody knows which languages were spoken in Caral or in the first Formative centers; the origin and expansion of Quechua and Aymara are debated (Torero, Cerrón-Palomino, Heggarty and Beresford-Jones, among others).

regiones/andes/idiomas.1.nota.texto: Quechua spread from central Peru centuries before the Incas, perhaps with Chavín or with Wari, with disputed dates (Torero, Cerrón-Palomino, Heggarty and Beresford-Jones); it is documented from Domingo de Santo Tomás (1560).

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/resumen.texto: The southern part of the Plata basin: the Argentine Littoral and Pampas, Uruguay and the area around Asunción. Inhabited by hunter-gatherers and Guaraní, it was colonized from 1536 from the Atlantic, became a viceroyalty in 1776 and went through the revolutions of independence from 1810.

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/eras.2.nombre.texto: Governorate of the Río de la Plata

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/eras.3.nombre.texto: Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/eras.0.resumen.texto: Hunter-gatherers of the Pampas (Querandí) and of the Banda Oriental (Charrúa), Guaraní and other peoples of the Littoral.

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/eras.1.resumen.texto: Solís reaches the Río de la Plata (1516); Asunción (1537) and the first Buenos Aires (1536).

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/eras.2.resumen.texto: Second founding of Buenos Aires by Garay and a long period on the periphery of the Spanish Empire.

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/eras.3.resumen.texto: Buenos Aires is the capital of the viceroyalty; the British invasions (1806-1807) weaken Spanish control.

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/eras.4.resumen.texto: May Revolution, independence in 1816, conflicts between Unitarians and Federalists.

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/eras.5.resumen.texto: Constitution of 1853 in Argentina; formation of the Argentine and Uruguayan states.

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/eras.6.resumen.texto: Massive immigration, agricultural expansion and urbanization. The Argentine crisis of 2001-2002, the Kirchnerist governments, those of Macri, Alberto Fernández and Milei in Argentina, and the alternation between the Frente Amplio and the traditional parties in Uruguay.

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/demografia.0.no.texto: All of Argentina (including the Northwest, Cuyo, the Chaco and Patagonia), Uruguay and Paraguay.

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/religiones.1.no.texto: Indigenous religions of the pampas and the southern Chaco

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/religiones.2.no.texto: About two-thirds of Argentines declare themselves Catholic; Uruguay has one of the highest proportions of non-believers in the Americas.

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/religiones.3.no.texto: The 1825 treaty with Great Britain guaranteed freedom of worship to British subjects.

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/religiones.4.no.texto: Argentina has the largest Jewish community in Latin America.

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/culturas.0.nomb.texto: Indigenous peoples (Querandíes, Charrúas, Chanás, Timbúes, Comechingones, Sanavirones, Tonocotés)

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/culturas.1.nomb.texto: Guaraní peoples (Paraguay, the Paraná and the islands)

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/culturas.2.nomb.texto: Spanish conquistadors (Buenos Aires, Asunción, Santiago del Estero)

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/culturas.4.nomb.texto: Encomended and reduced peoples (Guaraní, Comechingones, Tonocotés and others)

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/culturas.5.nomb.texto: Independent peoples of the pampas (Pampas and Tehuelches)

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/culturas.7.nomb.texto: Mapudungun-speaking peoples of the pampas (Ranqueles, Salinas Grandes)

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/culturas.11.nom.texto: Jews (agricultural colonies from 1889 and Buenos Aires)

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/culturas.0.nota.texto: Includes the builders of the littoral cerritos, from some 5,000 years ago.

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/culturas.3.nota.texto: In areas under Spanish control; the pampas and the southern Chaco remained in Indigenous hands.

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/culturas.6.nota.texto: In Buenos Aires they were about a third of the population at the end of the 18th century, according to the census rolls.

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/culturas.9.nota.texto: Together with the Spanish, the bulk of mass immigration.

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/culturas.10.not.texto: Counted are those who identify as Indigenous or as descendants of Indigenous peoples; they are a minority of the population.

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/idiomas.0.nombr.texto: Indigenous languages (Querandí, Charrúa, Chaná, Comechingón, Tonocoté and others)

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/idiomas.2.nombr.texto: Quechua (general language in colonial Tucumán; today in Santiago del Estero)

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/idiomas.1.nota.texto: In Paraguay it remained the language of the majority to this day. In Paraguay it is an official language alongside Spanish and is spoken by most of the population; it is also spoken in northeastern Argentina.

regiones/rio-de-la-plata/idiomas.2.nota.texto: It is still spoken in Santiago del Estero and among Andean migrants.

fuentes/epopeya-de-gilgamesh/resumen.texto: Epic poem about Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, his friendship with Enkidu and his quest for immortality. It exists in Sumerian versions, an Old Babylonian version (c. 1800 BC) and the so-called Standard version, known above all from the tablets of the library of Ashurbanipal in Nineveh.

fuentes/epopeya-de-gilgamesh/por_que_imp.texto: It is one of the oldest surviving literary works and contains a flood narrative that is compared with the one in Genesis. Its date of composition spans centuries of successive versions.

fuentes/epopeya-de-gilgamesh/leer.0.titu.texto: Old Babylonian version (Jastrow and Clay, 1920), Pennsylvania tablet

fuentes/codigo-de-hammurabi/soporte.texto: Diorite stele with 282 laws (now in the Louvre)

fuentes/codigo-de-hammurabi/resumen.texto: Collection of laws engraved by order of the king of Babylon, with a prologue and an epilogue. The stele was found in Susa in 1901, where it had been taken as booty.

fuentes/codigo-de-hammurabi/por_que_impo.texto: It shows how justice, social classes and property were conceived in 18th-century BC Mesopotamia, including the principle of retaliation (lex talionis).

fuentes/codigo-de-hammurabi/leer.0.titul.texto: Translation by L. W. King (Avalon Project, Yale University)

fuentes/lista-real-sumeria/resumen.texto: Record of the kings of Sumer with the length of each reign, beginning with a kingship “lowered from heaven” before the flood and reaching the Isin dynasty. It was compiled and expanded by scribes later than the events it recounts.

fuentes/lista-real-sumeria/por_que_impor.texto: It is the basis of Mesopotamian chronology, although it mixes historical and legendary kings and presents as successive dynasties that were in fact contemporaneous.

fuentes/lista-real-sumeria/leer.0.titulo.texto: The Sumerian king list: translation (ETCSL, University of Oxford)

fuentes/estela-de-mesha/soporte.texto: Basalt stele with 34 lines of text

fuentes/estela-de-mesha/resumen.texto: Inscription of King Mesha of Moab celebrating his victory over Israel and the rebuilding of cities. It was discovered in 1868 and is in the Louvre.

fuentes/estela-de-mesha/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the few extra-biblical sources that mentions Omri, king of Israel, and the name of Yahweh.

fuentes/estela-de-mesha/leer.0.titulo.texto: The Inscription on the Stele of Méšaʿ (Wikisource)

fuentes/guerra-de-los-judios/resumen.texto: An account of the Jewish revolt against Rome and the destruction of Jerusalem, written by a Jewish commander who defected to the Roman side. It includes the capture of Masada. In the speech he puts in the mouth of Agrippa II to dissuade the revolt (II.16.4), he says that the Gauls were guarded by only twelve hundred soldiers.

fuentes/guerra-de-los-judios/por_que_imp.texto: It is the main source on the war of 66-73 and the fall of the Second Temple, although it is written from the perspective of a protégé of the Flavians.

fuentes/guerra-de-los-judios/leer.0.titu.texto: The Wars of the Jews (translated by W. Whiston, Project Gutenberg)

fuentes/leyes-hititas/resumen.texto: Collection of some 200 provisions on homicide, theft, marriage, property and prices, recovered from the royal archive of Hattusa. It was copied for centuries.

fuentes/leyes-hititas/por_que_importa.texto: It allows Hittite law to be compared with Babylonian law: penalties are more often compensation than corporal punishment.

fuentes/anabasis/resumen.texto: Account of the expedition of ten thousand Greek mercenaries who supported Cyrus the Younger against his brother Artaxerxes II, and of their retreat from Babylon to the Black Sea. The author took part in it.

fuentes/anabasis/por_que_importa.texto: It is a direct testimony of the geography, peoples and roads of the Persian Empire and Anatolia around 400 BC.

fuentes/anabasis/leer.0.titulo.texto: Anabasis (translated by H. G. Dakyns, Project Gutenberg)

fuentes/res-gestae-divi-augusti/soporte.texto: Bronze inscription, copied in stone at Ancyra (Ankara) and other cities

fuentes/res-gestae-divi-augusti/resumen.texto: First-person summary of the deeds and expenditures of the emperor Augustus, written shortly before his death. The best-preserved text comes from the Temple of Rome and Augustus at Ancyra (present-day Ankara).

fuentes/res-gestae-divi-augusti/por_que_.texto: It shows how Augustus himself presented his rule, and its Anatolian copy is evidence of the spread of imperial propaganda.

fuentes/iliada/soporte.texto: Oral poem set down in writing; transmitted in papyrus scrolls

fuentes/iliada/resumen.texto: Epic poem in 24 books about the wrath of Achilles in the tenth year of the siege of Troy. It is attributed to Homer, but its composition and authorship are debated.

fuentes/iliada/por_que_importa.texto: It conveys the values and myths of Archaic Greece and was the basis of Greek education; it is not a chronicle of the Trojan War.

fuentes/iliada/leer.0.titulo.texto: Iliad, translated by A. T. Murray (Perseus, Tufts University)

fuentes/historias-herodoto/resumen.texto: Inquiry into the origins of the conflict between Greeks and Persians, with extensive descriptions of Egypt, Lydia, Persia and Scythia, and an account of the Persian Wars up to Plataea and Mycale.

fuentes/historias-herodoto/por_que_impor.texto: He is called the father of history; his digressions are the main source on many peoples of the 5th century BC. He mixes direct observation with accounts he himself says he does not believe. It is the oldest surviving work that names the Celts, alongside the sources of the Danube and the lands beyond the Pillars of Heracles, neighbors of the Cynetes (II.33; IV.49); the fragments of Hecataeus that also name them survive only through late quotations. He also recounts the voyages of the Phocaeans to Tartessos and its king Arganthonios (I.163–165).

fuentes/historias-herodoto/leer.0.titulo.texto: Histories, translated by A. D. Godley (Perseus, Tufts University)

fuentes/historias-herodoto/leer.1.titulo.texto: The History of Herodotus, translated by G. Rawlinson (Project Gutenberg)

fuentes/guerra-del-peloponeso/resumen.texto: Account of the war between Athens and Sparta, written by an Athenian general who lived through it; it breaks off in 411 BC. It includes speeches, among them Pericles' funeral oration.

fuentes/guerra-del-peloponeso/por_que_im.texto: It is the model of history based on eyewitnesses and on the analysis of political causes, and the central source for the 5th century BC.

fuentes/guerra-del-peloponeso/leer.0.tit.texto: History of the Peloponnesian War, translated by R. Crawley (Perseus, Tufts University)

fuentes/republica-platon/resumen.texto: Dialogue in ten books on justice, in which Socrates imagines an ideal city ruled by philosophers. It includes the allegory of the cave.

fuentes/republica-platon/por_que_importa.texto: It shows an Athenian's critique of his city's democracy and is a founding text of Western political philosophy.

fuentes/republica-platon/leer.0.titulo.texto: The Republic, translated by B. Jowett (Project Gutenberg)

fuentes/politica-aristoteles/resumen.texto: Treatise in eight books on the state, the types of constitution and the causes of revolutions. It drew on a study of some 158 constitutions of Greek cities, of which only that of Athens survives.

fuentes/politica-aristoteles/por_que_imp.texto: It defines the human being as a political animal and compares real constitutions; it is an indirect source on how the poleis functioned. In passing it names the Celts: among them love between men was openly honored (II.9, 1269b), they were among the peoples that honor war (VII.2, 1324b), and they kept newborns lightly wrapped to toughen them (VII.17, 1336a).

fuentes/politica-aristoteles/leer.0.titu.texto: Politics, translated by H. Rackham (Perseus, Tufts University)

fuentes/politica-aristoteles/leer.1.titu.texto: Politics: A Treatise on Government, translated by B. Jowett (Project Gutenberg)

fuentes/ab-urbe-condita/soporte.texto: Papyrus scrolls; only 35 of its 142 books survive

fuentes/ab-urbe-condita/resumen.texto: History of Rome from its legendary founding to the death of Drusus in 9 BC, in 142 books, of which books 1–10 and 21–45 survive. Livy wrote under Augustus and gathered earlier traditions and annalists. For almost all the lost books there are the Periochae, late summaries that are the only source for events such as the wars against the Allobroges and Arverni (121 BC), Arausio (105 BC) or the altar at Lugdunum.

fuentes/ab-urbe-condita/por_que_importa.texto: It is the main source on early monarchic and republican Rome, but it mixes legend and history and reflects the moral ideals of the principate. It recounts, always from Rome's side, the arrival of the Gauls in Italy and the sack of Rome (V.33–49), the duel of Manlius Torquatus with a Gaul (VII.9–10), the twin city, Greek and Iberian, of Emporion (XXXIV.9), and the campaign of Manlius Vulso against the Galatians (XXXVIII.12–27).

fuentes/ab-urbe-condita/leer.0.titulo.texto: Roman History, Books I-III (translated by G. Baker, Project Gutenberg)

fuentes/anales-tacito/resumen.texto: History of the Roman Empire from the death of Augustus (14) to that of Nero (68), in sixteen or eighteen books, of which books 1–6 and 11–16 survive, with gaps. Tacitus wrote between half a century and a century after the events, using Senate records and the works of earlier historians.

fuentes/anales-tacito/por_que_importa.texto: It offers a critical portrait of the Julio-Claudian emperors; it covers the fire of Rome in 64 and the persecution of Christians. It is also the main source on Caratacus (XII.31–40), on Boudica and the attack on the druids of Mona (XIV.29–37), on the uprising of Florus and Sacrovir in Gaul (III.40–46), and on Claudius's speech about the Gallic senators (XI.23–25), which also survives on the bronze tablet from Lyon.

fuentes/anales-tacito/leer.0.titulo.texto: Reign of Tiberius: Annals I-VI (Project Gutenberg)

fuentes/anales-tacito/leer.1.titulo.texto: Annals, English translation by Church and Brodribb (Perseus)

fuentes/anales-tacito/leer.2.titulo.texto: Book XII.37: Caratacus before Claudius (Perseus, Church and Brodribb)

fuentes/anales-tacito/leer.3.titulo.texto: Book XIV.31: the uprising of Boudica (Perseus, Church and Brodribb)

fuentes/guerra-de-las-galias/soporte.texto: Papyrus scrolls; transmitted in medieval codices

fuentes/guerra-de-las-galias/resumen.texto: Third-person account of Caesar's campaigns in Gaul from 58 to 52 BC, in seven books written by himself, year by year or all at once in the winter of 52–51 BC, which he spent at Bibracte (disputed); Book VIII, covering 51–50 BC, was added after his death by his officer Aulus Hirtius. Besides the military operations it includes an excursus on Gauls and Germans (VI.11–28), whose dependence on Posidonius is disputed (Tierney, 1960; Nash, 1976), with the druids who do not write down their doctrine but use Greek letters (VI.14), and the tablets of the Helvetii, also in Greek letters, with 368,000 emigrants (I.29).

fuentes/guerra-de-las-galias/por_que_imp.texto: It is almost the only source for the Roman conquest of Gaul and the first extensive description of the Gauls, written by the man who conquered them and for his career in Rome. Rambaud (1953) showed how he arranges and omits facts in his own favor, and his figures for enemies and dead are the most disputed (Henige, 1998).

fuentes/guerra-de-las-galias/leer.0.titu.texto: De Bello Gallico and other commentaries (Project Gutenberg)

fuentes/guerra-de-las-galias/leer.1.titu.texto: Commentaries on the Gallic War, translation by José Goya y Muniain (1919 edition, Wikisource)

fuentes/guerra-de-las-galias/leer.2.titu.texto: Latin text, Book I (The Latin Library)

fuentes/vidas-paralelas/resumen.texto: Paired biographies of a Greek and a Roman, from Theseus and Romulus to Antony. Plutarch wrote a few centuries after the events with moral aims, and drew on authors now lost.

fuentes/vidas-paralelas/por_que_importa.texto: It is the source of biographical data on many figures of ancient Greece and Rome, though it must be read with caution. On Gauls and Germans it recounts the sack of Rome (Camillus 15–32), the Cimbri and Teutones (Marius 11–27), the death of Viridomarus at Clastidium (Marcellus 6–8), and the conquest of Gaul with the figures that Caesar's propaganda circulated: eight hundred cities, three hundred peoples and a million dead (Caesar 15).

fuentes/vidas-paralelas/leer.0.titulo.texto: Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans (Dryden translation, Project Gutenberg)

fuentes/inscripcion-de-behistun/soporte.texto: Relief and trilingual inscription on a cliff measuring about 15 m by 25 m

fuentes/inscripcion-de-behistun/resumen.texto: Darius I recounts how he defeated the usurper Gaumata and the rebels of the empire. The text, in three languages, was copied in the 19th century by Henry Rawlinson, and its decipherment unlocked cuneiform.

fuentes/inscripcion-de-behistun/por_que_.texto: It is Darius's own direct testimony of his rise to the throne, and it was key to deciphering cuneiform, as the Rosetta Stone was for hieroglyphs.

fuentes/inscripcion-de-behistun/leer.0.t.texto: The Sculptures and Inscription of Darius the Great on the Rock of Behistûn (translated by L. W. King, Wikisource)

fuentes/gathas/soporte.texto: Oral transmission; written down in the Sasanian period

fuentes/gathas/resumen.texto: Seventeen hymns in Old Avestan, part of the Yasna, attributed to the prophet Zoroaster. They were transmitted orally for centuries and were only set down in writing in the Sasanian period.

fuentes/gathas/por_que_importa.texto: They are the oldest texts of the Zoroastrian tradition and among the few sources on Iranian religion before the Achaemenids; their dating is highly disputed.

fuentes/gathas/leer.0.titulo.texto: The Zend Avesta (translations by Darmesteter and Mills, Sacred Books of the East, Internet Archive)

fuentes/cilindro-de-ciro/soporte.texto: Clay cylinder in cuneiform script (British Museum)

fuentes/cilindro-de-ciro/resumen.texto: Proclamation written in the name of Cyrus II after the capture of Babylon, in which he presents himself as chosen by Marduk and lists his measures to restore temples and return displaced gods and peoples.

fuentes/cilindro-de-ciro/por_que_importa.texto: It is a direct source on the Persian conquest of Babylon, although its propagandistic nature is clear. Its reading as a declaration of human rights is disputed.

fuentes/shahnameh/resumen.texto: Epic poem of about 50,000 verses that tells the mythical and legendary history of Iran from the creation to the fall of the Sasanians to the Arabs. Ferdowsi completed it c. 1010.

fuentes/shahnameh/por_que_importa.texto: It is the great Persian national epic and a milestone of literary Persian; it gathers Sasanian traditions about the ancient kings.

fuentes/shahnameh/leer.0.titulo.texto: The Shah Nameh (translated by A. G. and E. Warner, Wikisource)

fuentes/analectas/autor.texto: Attributed to the disciples of Confucius

fuentes/analectas/resumen.texto: Short collection of sayings and dialogues of Confucius with his disciples, compiled over several generations after his death. Its twenty books deal with virtue, family, government and learning.

fuentes/analectas/por_que_importa.texto: It contains the foundation of Confucian thought, which shaped Chinese politics and education for more than two thousand years.

fuentes/analectas/leer.0.titulo.texto: The Analects of Confucius (translated by J. Legge, Project Gutenberg)

fuentes/shiji/resumen.texto: General history of China from the legendary Yellow Emperor to the reign of Han Wudi, in 130 chapters combining annals, tables, treatises and biographies. It continued a project begun by his father.

fuentes/shiji/por_que_importa.texto: It established the model of Chinese historiography and is the main source on pre-imperial China and the formation of the Han empire.

fuentes/daodejing/soporte.texto: Bamboo slips (Guodian manuscripts, c. 300 BC, and Mawangdui)

fuentes/daodejing/resumen.texto: Short book of some 81 chapters on the Dao, nature and effortless action (wu wei). Tradition attributes it to Laozi, but its author and date are uncertain.

fuentes/daodejing/por_que_importa.texto: It is the founding text of Taoism and one of the most translated works of world literature.

fuentes/daodejing/leer.0.titulo.texto: The Tao Teh King (translated by J. Legge, Project Gutenberg)

fuentes/el-arte-de-la-guerra/escrita.lug.texto: China (State of Qi or Wu, uncertain)

fuentes/el-arte-de-la-guerra/soporte.texto: Bamboo slips; Yinqueshan texts (2nd century BC)

fuentes/el-arte-de-la-guerra/resumen.texto: Treatise on military strategy attributed to Sunzi, who supposedly lived in the 6th century BC. Philological studies date its composition to between the 5th and 3rd centuries BC.

fuentes/el-arte-de-la-guerra/por_que_imp.texto: It shows the military thought of the Warring States period and its influence on politics and warfare in East Asia.

fuentes/el-arte-de-la-guerra/leer.0.titu.texto: The Art of War (translated by L. Giles, Project Gutenberg)

fuentes/rigveda/soporte.texto: Oral transmission for centuries; medieval manuscripts

fuentes/rigveda/resumen.texto: Collection of 1,028 hymns in ten books dedicated to Agni, Indra, Soma and other deities. It is the oldest text of the Vedic tradition and was transmitted orally for centuries.

fuentes/rigveda/por_que_importa.texto: It is the main source on the religion and society of the Indo-Aryan peoples of northern India; its dates are inferred from linguistics.

fuentes/rigveda/leer.0.titulo.texto: The Hymns of the Rigveda (translated by R. T. H. Griffith, Wikisource)

fuentes/edictos-de-ashoka/idioma_origina.texto: Prakrit (Brahmi and Kharosthi), Greek and Aramaic

fuentes/edictos-de-ashoka/soporte.texto: Inscriptions on rocks and polished sandstone pillars

fuentes/edictos-de-ashoka/resumen.texto: Edicts engraved by Ashoka Maurya on rocks and pillars throughout his empire, proclaiming his remorse for the Kalinga war and his policy of dhamma (piety, tolerance and non-violence). Some are in Greek and Aramaic.

fuentes/edictos-de-ashoka/por_que_import.texto: They are the oldest historically datable written documents of India, and direct evidence of how the king wished to be seen.

fuentes/edictos-de-ashoka/leer.0.titulo.texto: The Edicts of King Asoka (translated by S. Dhammika)

fuentes/arthashastra/resumen.texto: Treatise on politics, economics, espionage, law and war. Tradition attributes it to Kautilya, minister of Chandragupta Maurya, but specialists consider it a compilation from between the 2nd century BC and the 3rd century AD.

fuentes/arthashastra/por_que_importa.texto: It describes how a state was conceived in ancient India, with taxes, officials and strategy; its authorship and date are disputed.

fuentes/codice-florentino/titulo.texto: Florentine Codex (General History of the Things of New Spain)

fuentes/codice-florentino/autor.texto: Bernardino de Sahagún and Nahua collaborators

fuentes/codice-florentino/soporte.texto: Illustrated manuscript in 12 books, with more than 2,000 images (Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Florence)

fuentes/codice-florentino/resumen.texto: Encyclopedia of Mexica life, written in Nahuatl with the help of elders and students of the Colegio de Santa Cruz. It covers the gods, festivals, society, nature and, in Book XII, the conquest as seen by the vanquished.

fuentes/codice-florentino/por_que_import.texto: It is the richest source on Mexica society, with Indigenous voices, although it was compiled by a friar and decades after the conquest.

fuentes/popol-vuh/idioma_original.texto: K'iche' (with copy and translation by Ximénez, c. 1700)

fuentes/popol-vuh/soporte.texto: Alphabetic manuscript in K'iche'; the known copy is by Father Francisco Ximénez

fuentes/popol-vuh/resumen.texto: Sacred book of the K'iche' Maya that narrates the creation of the world, the adventures of the twins Hunahpú and Xbalanqué and the genealogy of the K'iche' lords. The lost original was written in the Latin alphabet around the mid-16th century.

fuentes/popol-vuh/por_que_importa.texto: It is the best written source on Maya mythology; it shows the Indigenous oral tradition about their own past.

fuentes/cartas-de-relacion/soporte.texto: Manuscript and printed letters to Emperor Charles V

fuentes/cartas-de-relacion/resumen.texto: Five letters to the king of Spain in which Cortés recounts the expedition to and conquest of Mexico, with descriptions of Tenochtitlan, its market and the peoples he encountered.

fuentes/cartas-de-relacion/por_que_impor.texto: It is a first-hand account of the conquest written by its main protagonist, with his own justifications and omissions.

fuentes/cartas-de-relacion/leer.0.titulo.texto: Letters and reports of Hernán Cortés to Emperor Charles V (Wikisource)

fuentes/comentarios-reales/resumen.texto: History of Inca Peru written by the son of a Spanish captain and a ñusta, a woman of the Inca nobility, which gathers family traditions and his childhood in Cusco. The second part, “General History of Peru,” recounts the conquest.

fuentes/comentarios-reales/por_que_impor.texto: It is the most influential source on the Tawantinsuyu. Much criticism points out that it idealizes the Inca past, and it was written in Spain, decades after the conquest.

fuentes/nueva-coronica-y-buen-gobierno/s.texto: Manuscript of some 1,200 pages with 398 drawings (Royal Library, Copenhagen)

fuentes/nueva-coronica-y-buen-gobierno/r.texto: Letter to King Philip III in which an Indigenous nobleman denounces colonial abuses and recounts Andean history from an Indigenous point of view, with hundreds of drawings.

fuentes/nueva-coronica-y-buen-gobierno/p.texto: It is one of the few written Andean voices from the first colonial century, and it combines text and image in a unique way.

fuentes/nueva-coronica-y-buen-gobierno/l.texto: Digital edition of the Royal Danish Library

fuentes/cronica-del-peru-cieza/resumen.texto: Description of the provinces of Peru, their roads, peoples and customs, based on the author's travels between 1535 and 1550. Cieza traveled the territory shortly after the conquest.

fuentes/cronica-del-peru-cieza/por_que_i.texto: It is one of the best first-hand descriptions of the Andean world just after the fall of the Inca Empire.

fuentes/cronica-del-peru-cieza/leer.0.ti.texto: The Travels of Pedro de Cieza de León, part of the Chronicle of Peru (translated by C. Markham, 1864, Internet Archive)

fuentes/viaje-al-rio-de-la-plata/titulo.texto: Voyage to the Río de la Plata

fuentes/viaje-al-rio-de-la-plata/soporte.texto: Manuscript; first printed edition in Frankfurt in 1567

fuentes/viaje-al-rio-de-la-plata/resumen.texto: First-person account by a Bavarian soldier who accompanied Pedro de Mendoza's expedition (1534) and lived almost twenty years in the Río de la Plata and Paraguay. It describes the first founding of Buenos Aires and the Indigenous peoples.

fuentes/viaje-al-rio-de-la-plata/por_que.texto: It is the fullest eyewitness account of the founding of Buenos Aires in 1536; it must be read with care because of its figures and the author's point of view.

fuentes/viaje-al-rio-de-la-plata/leer.0..texto: Voyage to the Río de la Plata and Paraguay (Wikisource)

fuentes/acta-de-independencia-1816/titul.texto: Declaration of Independence of the United Provinces of South America

fuentes/acta-de-independencia-1816/sopor.texto: Handwritten act; Quechua and Aymara version

fuentes/acta-de-independencia-1816/resum.texto: Act signed on 9 July 1816 by the deputies of the Congress of Tucumán. It declares the United Provinces “a free and independent nation from King Ferdinand VII, his successors and metropolis”; on 19 July the Congress added to the oath “and from all other foreign domination”.

fuentes/acta-de-independencia-1816/por_q.texto: It is the founding document of Argentine independence and shows the political language of the criollos.

fuentes/acta-de-independencia-1816/leer..texto: Declaration of Independence of the United Provinces of South America (Wikisource)

fuentes/actas-capitulares-mayo-1810/sopo.texto: Handwritten minute book of the Cabildo

fuentes/actas-capitulares-mayo-1810/resu.texto: Minutes of the Cabildo of Buenos Aires for the days of the open cabildo of 22 May and the formation of the Primera Junta on 25 May 1810.

fuentes/actas-capitulares-mayo-1810/por_.texto: They make it possible to reconstruct the May Revolution step by step as recorded by the body that governed it.

fuentes/facundo/titulo.texto: Facundo, or Civilization and Barbarism in the Argentine Pampas

fuentes/facundo/soporte.texto: Book printed in Santiago (first published in installments in El Progreso)

fuentes/facundo/resumen.texto: Essay-biography of Facundo Quiroga, a caudillo from La Rioja, describing the landscape, human types and politics of Rosas-era Argentina through the opposition between “civilization and barbarism”.

fuentes/facundo/por_que_importa.texto: It is a classic of Argentine literature and a source on the ideas of the liberal elite in exile; it is partial and controversial.

fuentes/martin-fierro/soporte.texto: Narrative poem in two parts (1872 and 1879)

fuentes/martin-fierro/resumen.texto: Verse poem telling the life of a gaucho forcibly conscripted for the frontier, his desertion and his life among the Indians. It gathers the grievances against the levy system and the treatment of gauchos.

fuentes/martin-fierro/por_que_importa.texto: It portrays the rural world of the Pampas frontier and was written while events were unfolding; it is a literary work, not a document.

fuentes/guerra-civil-cesar/soporte.texto: Papyrus rolls; transmitted in medieval codices

fuentes/guerra-civil-cesar/resumen.texto: Caesar's account, in three books, of his war against Pompey and the Senate in 49 and 48 BC, from shortly before crossing the Rubicon to the battle of Pharsalus and Pompey's flight to Egypt. It recounts the Spanish campaign (Ilerda), the siege of Massilia, Curio's disaster in Africa and the pursuit of Pompey in Greece. It has an abrupt ending and at least sixteen lost passages, so it may have been left unfinished; the oldest manuscripts date from the 10th century. It is continued by the Alexandrian, African and Spanish Wars, whose authorship is divided between Hirtius and others.

fuentes/guerra-civil-cesar/por_que_impor.texto: It is the only source for many of the events it narrates, and it was written by the victor: Caesar presents himself as the victim of a conspiracy by his enemies, justifies his acts as a defense of his dignity and of the peace of Rome, and omits military details. Like the Gallic War, it is read both as a campaign report and as propaganda.

fuentes/guerra-civil-cesar/leer.0.titulo.texto: De Bello Gallico and Other Commentaries, with the Civil War (Project Gutenberg)

fuentes/guerra-civil-cesar/leer.2.titulo.texto: Latin text, Book I (The Latin Library)

personas/hammurabi/resumen.texto: Sixth king of the First Dynasty of Babylon (c. 1792–1750 BC, middle chronology). He conquered the rival cities of the south and north and unified Mesopotamia under his rule; he left a famous law code.

personas/asurbanipal/resumen.texto: Last great king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire (c. 669–631 BC). He assembled in Nineveh a library of thousands of tablets, including the standard version of the Epic of Gilgamesh.

personas/nabucodonosor-ii/resumen.texto: King of Babylon (605–562 BC). He rebuilt the capital with its walls and the Ishtar Gate, and took Jerusalem in 597 and 587/586 BC.

personas/josefo/resumen.texto: Jewish priest from Jerusalem and commander in Galilee during the revolt of 66. Captured by the Romans, he settled in Rome under the Flavians and wrote “The Jewish War” and “Antiquities of the Jews”.

personas/herodes-el-grande/resumen.texto: King of Judea under Roman protection (37–4 BC). He rebuilt the Temple of Jerusalem and built Caesarea Maritima and the fortress of Masada. Augustus gave him the guard of four hundred Galatians that Cleopatra had had (Josephus, Jewish War I.397; Antiquities XV.217).

personas/saladino/resumen.texto: Founder of the Ayyubid dynasty. He unified Egypt and Syria, defeated the crusaders at Hattin (1187) and recovered Jerusalem.

personas/creso/resumen.texto: Last king of Lydia (c. 560–546 BC), famed for his wealth. Herodotus relates that he was defeated by Cyrus II and that his kingdom passed to Persia.

personas/pablo-de-tarso/resumen.texto: Hellenized Jew born in Cilicia. After his conversion he traveled through Anatolia, Greece and Italy, founding Christian communities; his letters are the oldest writings in the New Testament. Whether his letter to the Galatians was addressed to the northern Galatians, around Ancyra, or to the cities of the southern part of the province of Galatia that he visited on his first journey is disputed; W. M. Ramsay defended the second option.

personas/ataturk/resumen.texto: Military leader of the Turkish War of Independence and first president of the Republic of Turkey (1923–1938), who promoted secular reforms and the adoption of the Latin alphabet.

personas/herodoto/resumen.texto: Born in Halicarnassus, in Caria, he traveled through Egypt, Phoenicia, Mesopotamia and the Black Sea. His Histories, on the Persian Wars and the peoples of the known world, earned him the title of father of history.

personas/tucidides/resumen.texto: Athenian who commanded a fleet in 424 BC and was exiled after failing at Amphipolis. He wrote the history of the Peloponnesian War, which he witnessed.

personas/platon/resumen.texto: Disciple of Socrates and teacher of Aristotle; he founded the Academy in Athens. His dialogues, among them the Republic, are the foundation of Western philosophy.

personas/aristoteles/resumen.texto: Born in Stagira, he studied for twenty years at the Academy, was tutor to Alexander the Great and founded the Lyceum in Athens. He wrote on logic, physics, biology, ethics and politics.

personas/julio-cesar/resumen.texto: He conquered Gaul (58–50 BC), defeated Pompey in the civil war and was named perpetual dictator; he was assassinated on the Ides of March, 44 BC. Earlier, as governor of Hispania Ulterior (61–60 BC), he attacked the Lusitanians of the Herminian mountains and reached Brigantium by sea (Cassius Dio XXXVII.52–53). His Commentaries are almost the only source for the conquest of Gaul, and he wrote them for his political career (Rambaud, 1953; Riggsby, 2006). The figures of Plutarch (Caesar 15: a million dead and another million captives) and of Pliny (VII.92: 1,192,000 dead) cannot be verified and are read as propaganda; whether the conquest was a genocide is debated (Raaflaub, 2021).

personas/augusto/resumen.texto: Adoptive son of Caesar and the first emperor of Rome (27 BC–AD 14). He ended the civil wars and established the principate. He personally led the war against the Cantabrians and Astures in 26–25 BC (Suetonius, Augustus 20; Cassius Dio LIII.25), which his legates brought to an end in 19 BC.

personas/tito-livio/resumen.texto: Historian born in Patavium. He lived in Rome under Augustus and wrote the monumental history of Rome Ab urbe condita.

personas/tacito/resumen.texto: Roman senator and orator. Author of the Annals, the Histories, the Germania and the Agricola.

personas/ciro-ii/resumen.texto: Founder of the Achaemenid Empire: he defeated the Medes (c. 550 BC), Lydia (546) and Babylon (539). He died in battle against the Massagetae.

personas/dario-i/resumen.texto: King of Persia from 522 to 486 BC. He organized the empire into satrapies, minted coinage, began Persepolis and invaded Greece, where he was defeated at Marathon.

personas/firdusi/resumen.texto: Persian poet from Khorasan, author of the Shahnameh, which he composed over some thirty years.

personas/confucio/resumen.texto: Teacher of the Spring and Autumn period. His doctrine, centered on virtue, filial piety and good government, later became the core of imperial education and administration.

personas/sima-qian/resumen.texto: Grand historian of the Han court. Sentenced to castration for defending a general, he completed the Records of the Grand Historian. His birth is placed between 145 and 135 BC.

personas/qin-shi-huang/resumen.texto: King of Qin who unified China in 221 BC and proclaimed himself first emperor. He standardized writing, weights and measures and began the Great Wall and his mausoleum with the Terracotta Army.

personas/ashoka/resumen.texto: Maurya emperor (c. 268–232 BC). After the bloody conquest of Kalinga he turned to Buddhism and spread the dhamma through his edicts.

personas/aryabhata/resumen.texto: Astronomer and mathematician of the Gupta period. In the Aryabhatiya he proposes a value of pi, the rotation of the Earth and methods of trigonometric calculation.

personas/akbar/resumen.texto: Third Mughal emperor (1556–1605). He expanded the empire to cover almost all of northern India and practiced religious tolerance.

personas/moctezuma-ii/resumen.texto: Ninth tlatoani of Tenochtitlan (1502–1520). He received Cortés in 1519 and died in disputed circumstances during the fighting of 1520.

personas/hernan-cortes/resumen.texto: Conquistador from Extremadura who led the expedition against the Mexica (1519–1521) with the support of allied Indigenous peoples, and was governor of New Spain.

personas/bernardino-de-sahagun/resumen.texto: Franciscan who arrived in New Spain in 1529. He devoted decades to recording Nahua culture with the help of Indigenous informants and students.

personas/inca-garcilaso/resumen.texto: Son of a Spanish captain and the ñusta Chimpu Ocllo. Born in Cusco, he settled in Spain in 1560 and wrote there about the Incas.

personas/guaman-poma/resumen.texto: Indigenous nobleman from the Huamanga region. He wrote and illustrated the New Chronicle and Good Government, which was not published in his lifetime.

personas/atahualpa/resumen.texto: Last ruler of the Inca Empire, who won the civil war against his brother Huáscar. He was captured by Francisco Pizarro in Cajamarca in 1532 and executed in 1533.

personas/pachacutec/resumen.texto: Ninth Inca according to the chronicles, who led the great expansion of Tawantinsuyu from 1438 and remodeled Cusco. The dates of his reign come from oral tradition and are approximate.

personas/ulrico-schmidl/resumen.texto: Bavarian soldier who took part in Mendoza's expedition and in those of Paraguay (1534–1554). He wrote the account of his journey.

personas/juan-de-garay/resumen.texto: A Basque who lived in Asunción, he founded Santa Fe (1573) and the second Buenos Aires (1580). He died in 1583 in an Indigenous attack.

personas/sarmiento/resumen.texto: A native of San Juan, he was exiled in Chile between 1840 and 1851, where he wrote Facundo (1845) and Viajes y Recuerdos de provincia.
